Q: Clarification on JOIN statements SQL A:

Every Join creates a cartesian product (like a cross join) of the two tables that are being joined, BUT ... ON limits where that cartesian product is being applied by adding conditions.

E.g.

ON orders.warehouse_id = warehouse.warehouse_id

means that the Join will only create cartesian products where the warehouse_id in orders matches the warehouse_id in warehouse. Ideally, in both tables there is only one row with the same id each. But, if there were to be more rows in both tables, you'd get the cross product. E.g. 3 rows with warehouse_id 23 in orders and 2 rows with the same id in warehouse would result in 2*3 = 6 rows with warehouse_id 23 in your result table.

The kind of join (LEFT/RIGHT/FULL OUTER/INNER) just defines what happens when there is no match in either of the tables for a certain id from the other table. E.g. LEFT JOIN keeps all the rows in the left table although they don't have a match in the right table. INNER JOIN doesn't keep any rows without match - it still applies cartesian products (basically cross joins) within the bounds of the ON conditions.

If you just join ON true, e.g. in a full outer join, you will get a cartesian product including all (depending on the kind of join) unmatched rows.

Q: What are C++ interviews like for semiconductor/GPU companies A:

A former coworker of mine drove that same point home. Over and over.

STL is not the Standard C++ Library. The Standard C++ Library is not STL. STL has pretty much stopped being maintained over 2 decades ago. Only about a third of the STL was incorporated into C++98.

(My former coworker was Alex Stepanov. Fun triva fact: STL was originally written in Ada.)

Q: How do I solve this type hint error "Unexpected type(s)" in PyCharm? A:

The variable redefinition seems to be the main problem. I recommend avoiding the re-assignment in this case, since working around it seems more troublesome than worth it.

From what I've gathered in the comments, the current filename variable (used in the if clause, and on the right side of the assignment to the new variable), is atually more akin to something like filename_suffix (or suffix for short).

Inlining the exerpt you mentioned in your comments, and presuming the type of datum_content_type to be str, we get:

import datetime

from typing import reveal_type

suffix: str | None = None
datum_content_type: str = ''

if suffix: #  i.e. not None
    fn = str(datetime.datetime.now()).replace(":", "-").replace(".", "-") + " - " + datum_content_type + " - " + suffix
    reveal_type(fn) # `str` in PyCharm's inlay hint, corroborated by MyPy.
    with open("files\\" + fn, "wb") as f:
        pass

With no more warnings in the with line :)

Two (tangential) notes:

  1. Please be aware that checking if s: ..., when s is str | None, does not execute the code block if the s is an empty string. This behavior may be desired or not, but be mindful of it. This may trip you up if you come from a C background.

  2. I strongly recommend explicitly choosing how your timestamps are formatted with strftime, instead of relying on the default behavior of datetime.__str__, which is to invoke datetime.isoformat. Luckily (?), in Python, the datetime objects returned by datetime.now are always timezone-naïve, which means consistent string formatting. However, in other languages or scenarios, not explicitly specifying whether to include the timezone in the formatted string can cause a world of hurt later on. This would also have the added benefit of removing the need for the str.replace calls, since you can just set the desired separator(s) in the format template directly :D
